exercises.prompt: You run `as --64 -o prog.o prog.s` and then `ld -o prog prog.o`. What does each step produce?

options.label: `as` produces an object file of machine code; `ld` combines object files into an executable the system can run.
options.feedback: Yes. The assembler translates instructions and directives into bytes; the linker fixes up addresses between files, chooses where each section lives and writes the executable.

options.label: `as` runs the program; `ld` lists its machine code.
options.feedback: Not yet. Neither tool runs anything. `objdump -d` is the tool that lists machine code.

options.label: `as` produces the executable; `ld` is only needed for programs that use the C library.
options.feedback: Not yet. Even our library-free programs need `ld`: an object file is not executable until a linker has given it addresses and an entry point.

options.label: `as` compiles the program to C; `ld` compiles the C to machine code.
options.feedback: Not yet. No C is involved: assembly is translated directly to machine code, almost line for line.

hints: One of the two tools turns text into bytes. The other turns one or more files of bytes into something you can start with `./prog`.
exercises.solution: `as` reads the assembly text and writes an **object file** (`prog.o`): machine code and data, with some addresses still unresolved. `ld` reads one or more object files, places each section at an address, resolves the references between them, records the entry point `_start`, and writes the **executable** `prog`.

exercises.prompt: On x86-64 Linux, which number goes into `rax` (or `eax`) to make the `exit` system call?

feedback.message: Not yet: 1 is `write`. Look at the last three lines of the hello program.
Not yet: 0 is the exit *status* we pass in `edi`. The call number goes in `eax`.

hints: Look for the comment `# exit(0)` in the first program.
exercises.solution: **60.** The program ends with `mov eax, 60`, `xor edi, edi`, `syscall`: call number 60 (`exit`) with status 0. Numbers are specific to Linux on x86-64; ARM64 and RISC-V Linux use 93 for the same call.

exercises.prompt:
What value does the assembler give `len` here?

```asm
msg:    .ascii "Salaam\n"
        .equ len, . - msg
```

feedback.message: Not yet: count the newline `\n` too. It is one byte, the number 10.
Not yet: `.ascii` does not add a terminating zero byte (`.asciz` would).

hints: `.` is the address just after the last byte of the string.
Count the letters, then the newline.
exercises.solution: "Salaam" is 6 bytes and `\n` is 1 more, so `. - msg` is **7**. `.ascii` adds no zero byte at the end, unlike `.asciz`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print? (Type the visible characters, without the newline.)

```asm
        .intel_syntax noprefix
        .section .rodata
msg:    .ascii "Bonjour, monde!\n"

        .text
        .globl _start
_start:
        mov     eax, 1
        mov     edi, 1
        lea     rsi, [rip + msg + 9]
        mov     edx, 7
        syscall

        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

feedback.message: Not yet: the write starts 9 bytes after `msg`, not at `msg`.
Close: 7 bytes starting at offset 9 include the `!` (and the newline).

hints: Number the bytes from 0: B is 0, o is 1, … the comma is 7, the space is 8.
Seven bytes starting at offset 9: which characters are they?
exercises.solution: Offsets 0–6 are `Bonjour`, 7 is the comma, 8 the space, so offset 9 is the `m` of `monde`. Seven bytes from there are `m o n d e ! \n`, so the program prints **monde!** followed by a newline.

exercises.prompt:
This program's message is written as numbers. What does it print? (Without the newline.)

```asm
        .intel_syntax noprefix
        .section .rodata
reply:  .byte 0x4F, 0x6B, 0x21, 10

        .text
        .globl _start
_start:
        mov     eax, 1
        mov     edi, 1
        lea     rsi, [rip + reply]
        mov     edx, 4
        syscall
        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

Useful codes: 0x41 is `A`, 0x61 is `a`, 0x21 is `!`.
hints: 0x4F is 0x41 + 14. Which capital letter is 14 after A?
0x6B is 0x61 + 10. Which lowercase letter is 10 after a?
exercises.solution: 0x4F = 0x41 + 14 is `O`, 0x6B = 0x61 + 10 is `k`, 0x21 is `!` and 10 is the newline. The program prints **Ok!**. Text in memory is only numbers; the terminal turns the codes into letters.

exercises.prompt: A friend copies the `hello` executable from this lesson to three machines. On which one will it run unchanged?

options.label: A cloud server with an AMD EPYC (x86-64) processor running Ubuntu Linux.
options.feedback: Yes. Same processor family and same operating system: the instructions and the system-call numbers both match.

options.label: A Raspberry Pi 5 running Linux.
options.feedback: Not yet. The Raspberry Pi 5 has an ARM64 processor. It cannot decode x86-64 machine code, even though Linux is there.

options.label: A Windows laptop with an Intel x86-64 processor, outside WSL.
options.feedback: Not yet. The processor understands every instruction, but Windows uses a different executable format and different system calls, so the program cannot even be loaded.

options.label: All three, because assembly is the most portable language.
options.feedback: Not yet. Assembly is the *least* portable language: it is tied to one processor family and, once it makes system calls, to one operating system.

hints: Two things must match: the processor family that decodes the bytes, and the operating system that answers the system calls.
exercises.solution: Only the **x86-64 Linux server**. The Raspberry Pi has the right operating system but the wrong processor family; the Windows laptop has the right processor but the wrong operating system (different executable format and system calls). Inside WSL 2 on that laptop the program would run, because WSL 2 is a real Linux kernel.

exercises.prompt: You delete the last three lines (the `exit` system call) from the hello program, then assemble, link and run it. What happens?

options.label: It prints the message and then crashes, typically with a segmentation fault.
options.feedback: Yes. After the `write`, the processor keeps fetching whatever bytes follow `_start`'s code, which are not a sensible program, until something faults.

options.label: It prints the message and returns to the shell normally, like a C `main` that ends.
options.feedback: Not yet. A C `main` returns to the C library, which then calls `exit` for you. `_start` has no caller to return to.

options.label: The assembler refuses to assemble a program without `exit`.
options.feedback: Not yet. The assembler translates what you write; it does not know or check that a program must end with a system call.

options.label: Nothing is printed, because the output is only flushed at exit.
options.feedback: Not yet. `write` is a direct system call: the bytes reach the terminal as soon as it returns. Output buffering is a feature of libraries such as C's stdio.

hints: What instruction does the processor run after the second-to-last `syscall`, once the exit code is gone?
exercises.solution: The `write` succeeds, so the message appears. Then the processor fetches the next bytes after the code, which are padding or other data, and runs them as instructions. Very soon it executes something invalid or touches an unmapped address, and Linux kills the program with a **segmentation fault** (or an illegal-instruction signal). A program with no C library must always end with the `exit` system call.
